newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks place in history with budget law.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks place in history with budget law.

text.p: Seeking to solidify his place in history, President Bill Clinton on Tuesday will sign landmark legislation that aims to balance the U.S. budget and cut taxes at the same time.

The legislation was approved by the Republican-controlled Congress last week, and to show the bipartisan nature of the bill, the White House has invited House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich to join Clinton in making remarks at the South Lawn ceremony.

Vice President Al Gore will also speak, as will the ranking Democrat on the Senate Budget Committee, Sen. Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey. Among the expected crowd of 700 will be members of Congress, Cabinet officers, and representatives from labour, education, the elderly and other groups.

Enactment of the law may well be the crowning achievement of Clinton's second term as he attempts to secure a favourable place in history while presiding over a nation at peace and with a booming economy.

His agreement to enter into negotiations for a balanced budget was a stark turnabout for a Democratic president who had to be dragged into the debate by Republicans when they seized control of Congress in 1994.
The day before the ceremony, Clinton went to great pains to defend the budget plan against critics, who say its $95 billion in tax cuts are tilted toward the wealthy.

A $500-per-child tax credit will help the middle class, he told the National Urban League, such as "firefighters, police officers, nurses, teachers, technicians, people who deserve all the help they can get to raise their children."

And lest people think he knuckled under to Republican demands, Clinton said many Democratic goals were achieved in the bill. A $24 billion programme for children's health will be created, he noted, and new spending on education will be the most in over 30 years.
The legislation also takes some of the sting out of the welfare law Clinton signed last year by restoring benefits to legal immigrants.
"We have to be about the business of giving people the power to make the most of their own lives and their families and their neighbourhoods and their communities," he told the National Urban League.
The two opposing parties were helped along in their drive to balance the budget by a robust economy generating tax revenues that have already sliced the deficit this year to unheard-of levels.

The Treasury Department reported last month that the federal budget deficit shrank to $10.87 billion for the first nine months of the fiscal year. The United States has not posted a budget surplus since 1969.
Robert Reischauer, a budget analyst at the Brookings Institution think tank, called the budget deal historic but noted that "like most history, it has been built over a number of years."

Reischauer argued that the effort to balance the budget began with former President George Bush's decision to raise taxes in 1990, violating his "no new taxes" campaign promise. The move is widely credited with costing him the 1992 election.
It was given a push by Clinton's 1993 economic programme, which passed Congress without a single Republican vote, and by the Republican seizure of Congress the next year.
